chapterName: Early Republic: The Samnite Wars (367-290 BCE)

questions.question: When the Samnites trapped a Roman consul's army in a mountain pass in 343 BC, how did Publius Decius Mus save it?
options: He brought up reinforcements from Capua
He seized a hilltop and distracted the enemy
He bribed the Samnite commander to withdraw
He led the army out through a hidden tunnel
questions.explanation: Decius, then a junior officer, seized a hilltop with a small band and drew off the enemy while the army escaped. The trapped consul was Aulus Cornelius Cossus.
questions.sourceQuote: A junior officer, Publius Decius Mus, seized a hilltop with a small band and distracted the enemy while the army escaped.

questions.question: What lasting Roman innovation came out of the siege of Naples?
options: The appointment of emergency dictators
The creation of a permanent fleet
Extending a command with the title of proconsul
The election of two consuls each year
questions.explanation: Instead of handing over to the next year's consuls, the commanders kept their command until the campaign ended, as proconsuls. One of them was Quintus Publilius Philo.
questions.sourceQuote: Instead of handing over to the next year's consuls, the commanders, including Quintus Publilius Philo, had their military command extended until the campaign ended, with the title of proconsul.

questions.question: At Sentinum in 295 BC, what did the consul Publius Decius Mus do after Gallic chariots broke his wing?
options: He negotiated a truce with the Gauls
He handed his command to his colleague Fabius
He devoted himself and charged to his death
He retreated behind the Roman camp walls
questions.explanation: Decius prayed to the gods and charged into the enemy, sacrificing his life. His men rallied, and Fabius outflanked the Samnites to win the battle.
questions.sourceQuote: Decius then devoted himself: he prayed to the gods and charged into the enemy, sacrificing his life.

questions.question: What were the Caudine Forks, where a Roman army was trapped in 321 BC?
options: A marshy river crossing on the Liris
A dense forest just north of Rome
A narrow coastal pass near Cumae
Two wooded Apennine gorges joined by a ravine
questions.explanation: The Caudine Forks were two narrow wooded gorges in the Apennines joined by a tight ravine. The Samnites blocked both ends with felled trees and boulders.
questions.sourceQuote: The two consuls took the quickest road, through the Caudine Forks, two narrow wooded gorges in the Apennines joined by a tight ravine.

questions.question: What did elite Samnite units swear before the battle at Aquilonia in 293 BC?
options: To give no quarter to prisoners
To march on Rome itself
To sacrifice their spoils to the gods
Never to flee, on pain of death
questions.explanation: Elite units swore a sacred oath never to flee, on pain of death. Some 40,000 Samnites gathered at Aquilonia in north-western Samnium.
questions.sourceQuote: Elite units swore a sacred oath never to flee, on pain of death.

questions.question: Which river divided Latium, the Latin homeland around Rome, from Campania?
options: The Liris
The Arno
The Tiber
The Volturnus
questions.explanation: In the mid-fourth century BC, Rome's territory reached south as far as the River Liris, the boundary between Latium and Campania. Modern historians suspect the 354 BC treaty made it a dividing line between Rome and the Samnites.
questions.sourceQuote: This river divided Latium, the Latin homeland around Rome, from Campania, the fertile plain running down to the Bay of Naples.

questions.question: Where did Marcus Valerius Corvus win the first Roman victory of the First Samnite War?
options: Lautulae
Sentinum
Mount Gaurus
Suessula
questions.explanation: Valerius won at Mount Gaurus, near Cumae, with a desperate charge as daylight faded. Livy credits Rome with three victories in 343 BC.
questions.sourceQuote: Marcus Valerius Corvus won the first at Mount Gaurus, near the coastal town of Cumae, with a desperate charge as daylight faded.

questions.question: Which dreaded forest, never before crossed by a Roman, did Quintus Fabius Maximus Rullianus march his army through?
options: The Ciminian Forest
The Arsian Forest
The Sila Forest
The Hercynian Forest
questions.explanation: Fabius first sent his Etruscan-speaking brother, disguised as a shepherd, through the Ciminian Forest, then marched his army through it. This opened the way into Etruria.
questions.sourceQuote: Quintus Fabius Maximus Rullianus, Rome's leading general of the era, sent his Etruscan-speaking brother, disguised as a shepherd, through the dreaded Ciminian Forest, which no Roman had ever crossed.
reviewFlags: fact-check: The explanation claims the march 'opened the way into Etruria', which the chapter does not state.

questions.question: Why do most historians now accept that the First Samnite War really happened?
options: Diodorus describes it in great detail
No Roman would invent a story so embarrassing
Archaeologists have found its battlefields
Greek inscriptions record its peace treaty
questions.explanation: The war's embarrassing details make it unlikely to be a Roman invention. Some historians once rejected it entirely because Diodorus never mentions it.
questions.sourceQuote: Most now accept it: no Roman would invent a story so embarrassing to Rome.

questions.question: Which city provided the spark for the Second Samnite War?
options: Naples
Cumae
Luceria
Capua
questions.explanation: Naples, then a Greek city, was the spark: Livy says its old town, Paleopolis, attacked Romans living in Campania. Samnite troops helped defend the city against Rome.
questions.sourceQuote: The spark came from Naples, then a Greek city made up of an old town, Paleopolis, and a newer one, Neapolis.
